entities.summary:
Nostrianus, Bishop of Naples from approximately 432 to 452 CE, emerged as a pivotal figure in the Western Roman Empire during a period of profound theological dispute and escalating barbarian incursions. His episcopacy coincided with the final decades of imperial authority in Italy, a time when the Nicene Christian orthodoxy faced severe challenges from Arianism and the burgeoning Pelagian controversy. Nostrianus distinguished himself not only as a staunch defender of the Council of Nicaea's doctrines but also as a compassionate leader, providing crucial humanitarian aid and spiritual solace amidst the chaos of the Vandal Age.

The most notable event of Nostrianus's tenure occurred in 439, following the Vandal King Gaiseric's capture and sacking of Carthage, the jewel of Roman Africa. This devastating blow prompted a mass exodus of Nicene clergy, including Bishop Quodvultdeus of Carthage, who was exiled with his clergy to Naples. Nostrianus, demonstrating remarkable courage and Christian charity, offered shelter and support to Quodvultdeus and his companions, allowing them to continue their ecclesiastical functions and preserving a vital fragment of African Christian leadership and tradition within Italy. This act not only provided immediate relief but also symbolized the resilience of the Nicene Church in the face of persecution.
